# How to store your token

Persist a Glassfrog API token once so the CLI authenticates later commands
without you re-supplying it. This guide covers every way to supply the token,
where it gets written, and how to replace one that already exists.

## Prerequisites

- The `glassfrog` executable on your `PATH`.
- The API token you want to store.

## Supply the token

The `glassfrog auth login` command accepts the token from the first available
source in this order: **command argument → piped stdin → `GLASSFROG_TOKEN` →
interactive prompt**. Pick whichever fits your situation.

### As a command argument

```
glassfrog auth login gf_live_yourtoken
```

### Piped on standard input (no terminal)

```
printf '%s' "$TOKEN" | glassfrog auth login
```

Use this in scripts and CI — the value is read from the pipe and never echoed.

### From the environment

If `GLASSFROG_TOKEN` is already set and you supply no argument and pipe nothing,
`login` persists that value:

```
GLASSFROG_TOKEN=gf_live_yourtoken glassfrog auth login
```

### Interactive prompt

If you're at a terminal and supply no token any other way, the CLI prompts for
it and does not echo what you type. (If standard input is **not** a terminal and
no token was supplied, the command fails with `no token to store` rather than
hanging — see Troubleshooting.)

## Choose where it's written

By default the token is written to `.glassfrogrc` in your home directory. To
write a project-local file in the current directory instead, add `--cwd`:

```
printf '%s' "$TOKEN" | glassfrog auth login --cwd
```

A current-directory file takes precedence over your home file when the CLI later
resolves a token, so `--cwd` is how you pin a project to its own token.

## Replace an existing token

What happens when a token is already stored depends on whether you're
interactive:

- **At a terminal**: the command confirms before changing anything, and — when
  tokens exist in both the current directory and home — offers to write the
  current-directory file, the home file, or both.
- **Non-interactive**: the command refuses to change an existing token unless you
  pass `--overwrite`. With `--overwrite` it merges into the single target
  location (home by default, or the current directory under `--cwd`):

```
printf '%s' "$NEW_TOKEN" | glassfrog auth login --overwrite
```

A merge replaces **only** the `token` entry — any other lines and comments in the
file are preserved.

## Verify

On success the command prints the path it wrote, never the token:

```
Stored credentials in /home/you/.glassfrogrc
```

The file is created readable only by its owner. You can confirm the stored value
round-trips by running any command that resolves credentials — it will report
the source as that file path.

## Troubleshooting

These messages go to **stderr**; the exit code follows the
[exit-code convention](../how-to-read-exit-codes.md).

| You see | Cause | Do this |
|---|---|---|
| `no token to store` | Non-interactive session and no token via argument, stdin, or `GLASSFROG_TOKEN` (exit `2`) | Supply a token by one of those sources |
| `the supplied token is not usable (empty, whitespace-only, or containing line breaks) …` | The token was empty, whitespace-only, or contained a line break (exit `2`) | Supply a single-line, non-empty token |
| `a credential already exists at <path>` | A token is already stored and the session is non-interactive without `--overwrite` (exit `2`) | Pass `--overwrite` to replace it |
| A write error naming `<path>` | The target location isn't writable (exit `1`) | Check write permission on the directory; `<path>` was not partially written (an interactive "both" write may have already written an earlier target) |
| A format error naming `<path>` | The existing `.glassfrogrc` couldn't be parsed for a merge (exit `1`) | Fix or remove the malformed file; it is not overwritten |

The token value never appears in any message, prompt, or success line.
